competency_fulfillment.rationale: The samples genuinely solve area problems, and in both directions. Forward, seed 604, 'Kris wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 8 m long and 5 m wide with square tiles that are 1 m on each side. How many tiles are needed to cover it completely?', is answerable from the stem alone — both dimensions and the tile size are given, so 8 × 5 = 40. Inverse, seed 50, 'A rectangle has an area of 21 sq m and a length of 3 m. What is its width?', makes the student work back through 21 ÷ 3 = 7. That is problem solving about area rather than tile-counting practice.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Squares and rectangles, the two figures the wording names, both carry real items: the square at seed 43, 'Kuya Bien wants to cover a square garden measuring 3 m on each side', and at seed 603, 'Yna wants to cover a square card measuring 5 cm on each side', with rectangles from seed 42 onward. Within the rectangle case both unknowns are exercised, the missing width at seed 44, 'A rectangle has an area of 15 sq cm and a length of 5 cm. What is its width?', and the missing length at seed 501, 'A rectangle has an area of 28 sq cm and a width of 4 cm. What is its length?'. The inverse direction is never applied to a square, though the wording does not name that sub-case.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Contexts are concrete, local and single-step — seed 46, 'Ate Cara wants to cover a square garden measuring 2 m on each side with square tiles that are 1 m on each side', and the 5 cm card at seed 603 — and the names Kuya Bien, Ate Cara, Pia and Yna sit naturally for a Filipino Grade 3 class. The word problems are all answerable from what they state; seed 42, 'Daniel wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 4 m long and 3 m wide with square tiles that are 1 m on each side', supplies every number needed and leaves no partial tile. The inverse items need one missing-factor division, 24 ÷ 3 = 8 at seed 502, which is within reach in Quarter 1.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: All fourteen samples come from exactly two sentence frames. Six are the tiling context of seed 601, 'Pia wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 2 m long and 3 m wide with square tiles that are 1 m on each side. How many tiles are needed to cover it completely?', with only the name, the shape and the two numbers changing. The other eight are the bare inverse of seed 600, 'A rectangle has an area of 18 sq m and a width of 3 m. What is its length?'. Nothing asks straight out for an area in square units, no item compares two figures or takes two steps, and no situation other than covering a garden or a card ever appears.

competency_alignment.rationale: Every item keeps the area relationship of a square or a rectangle as the thing being reasoned about, and none slips into perimeter or into bare multiplication practice. Seed 600, 'A rectangle has an area of 18 sq m and a width of 3 m. What is its length?', can only be answered by inverting area equals length times width, and seed 43, 'Kuya Bien wants to cover a square garden measuring 3 m on each side with square tiles that are 1 m on each side', is an applied covering problem rather than an exercise in illustrating or deriving a rule.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Magnitudes stay small and physically sensible. The largest computation is the 8 × 5 = 40 sq m at seed 604, and every division sits inside the basic facts — 30 ÷ 5 = 6 at seed 500, 'A rectangle has an area of 30 sq m and a width of 5 m. What is its length?', and 28 ÷ 4 = 7 at seed 501. Units fit the object measured: the card at seed 603 is '5 cm on each side' while the garden at seed 43 is '3 m on each side', so no sample asks a Grade 3 pupil to imagine a five-metre greeting card.
